propositions.text: This is a judicial review application under subsection 72(1) of IRPA challenging the RAD decision dismissing the appeal from the RPD decision.
propositions.quote: In this application for judicial review brought under subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], Denbel Bekelech challenges a decision rendered by the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD], which dismissed her appeal from a decision of the Refugee Protection Division [RPD] rejecting her claim for refugee protection.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, this application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review of the RAD decision dismissing the appeal from the RPD, and dismisses the application.

propositions.text: The applicant is an Ethiopian citizen of part Oromo and part Gurage ethnicity; her husband is Oromo.
propositions.quote: The applicant is a citizen of Ethiopia. Her ethnicity is part Oromo and part Gurage. The ethnicity of her husband is Oromo.

propositions.text: The Ethiopian authorities perceive her husband as a member of the OLF, engaged in armed struggle against the government.
propositions.quote: According to the applicant, the Ethiopian authorities perceive her husband as a member of the Oromo Liberation Front [OLF], a group that is currently engaged in armed struggle against the government.

propositions.text: The authorities arrested, imprisoned and tortured her husband in January 2012.
propositions.quote: She alleges that the authorities arrested, imprisoned and tortured her husband in January 2012.

propositions.text: After bail and release in June 2012, her husband disappeared to hide from authorities.
propositions.quote: After she posted bail and secured his release in June 2012, he disappeared to hide from the authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is Ethiopian of mixed ethnicity; the applicant alleges her husband was perceived as OLF member, arrested, tortured, and disappeared after release.

propositions.text: The applicant alleges she was arrested on July 11, 2012 and held for one month to draw out her husband.
propositions.quote: The applicant alleges that she was arrested on July 11, 2012 and held for one month because the authorities wanted to draw her husband out of hiding.

propositions.text: She alleges a second arrest on January 3, 2013, detained until January 5, 2013.
propositions.quote: She alleges that she was arrested a second time on January 3, 2013 and detained until January 5, 2013.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges two arrests: July 2012 for one month, and January 2013 for two days, aimed at drawing out her husband.

propositions.text: The applicant supports the opposition party UDJ, having voted and distributed pamphlets for it.
propositions.quote: The applicant also alleges that she supports an opposition party named Unity for Democracy and Justice [UDJ], having voted for it and distributed pamphlets on its behalf.

propositions.text: She attributes her persecution to her support for UDJ and her husband’s OLF affiliation.
propositions.quote: She attributes her persecution to her support for this party and her husband’s affiliation with the OLF.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges she supports UDJ and attributes persecution to her and her husband's political affiliations.

propositions.text: The applicant entered Canada on May 28, 2013 on a visa and applied for refugee protection due to political opinion.
propositions.quote: On May 28, 2013, the applicant entered Canada, where she has family, on a visa. Thereafter, she applied for refugee protection due to her political opinion.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant entered Canada on a visa in May 2013 and applied for refugee protection based on political opinion.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the refugee claim on September 6, 2013; the applicant appealed to RAD on December 20, 2013 and submitted appeal record January 6, 2014.
propositions.quote: The RPD rejected the applicant’s refugee claim in a decision dated September 6, 2013. The applicant filed a notice of appeal at the RAD on December 20, 2013. She submitted an appeal record on January 6, 2014.

propositions.text: The applicant moved to admit new evidence on January 31, 2014; RAD dismissed the appeal on April 10, 2014.
propositions.quote: On January 31, 2014, she brought a motion to admit new evidence to the RAD record. The RAD dismissed the applicant’s appeal by decision dated April 10, 2014.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the claim; the applicant appealed to RAD, moved to admit new evidence, but RAD dismissed the appeal.

propositions.text: The decision under review is the RAD decision, but the court begins with an overview of the RPD decision.
propositions.quote: While the decision under review, properly speaking, is the RAD decision, it makes sense to begin with an overview of the RPD decision.

propositions.text: The RPD panel found credibility was the determinative issue and drew negative inferences against the applicant’s credibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD panel declared that the determinative issue was credibility. It drew several negative inferences against Mrs Bekelech’s credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the RAD decision is under review but begins with the RPD decision, which found credibility was key and drew negative inferences.

propositions.text: The applicant was inconsistent about circumstances of her arrest; BOC said two arrests with police station reporting, hearing said police came at night.
propositions.quote: First, the applicant was inconsistent about the circumstances surrounding her arrest. In her basis of claim form [BOC], she stated that she had been arrested twice. After her first arrest, she had been told to report to the police station regularly, and she was arrested a second time in January 2013 while reporting. At the hearing, the applicant testified that the police had come to her home at night to arrest her the second time.

propositions.text: The applicant could not explain this contradiction to the panel’s satisfaction.
propositions.quote: She could not explain this contradiction to the panel’s satisfaction.

propositions.text: The panel considered this contradiction highly material as the second arrest motivated her to seek refuge.
propositions.quote: The panel considered this contradiction highly material because her second arrest was the event which allegedly motivated her to seek refuge in another country.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the applicant inconsistent about her second arrest circumstances and considered this contradiction highly material.

propositions.text: The applicant was inconsistent about reasons for police arrest; BOC said distributing UDJ flyers, hearing said she did not distribute flyers and did not know why arrested.
propositions.quote: Second, the applicant was inconsistent about the reasons the police arrested her. In her BOC, she stated that the police arrested her in January 2013 because they believed that she had been distributing political flyers for the UDJ party. At the hearing, the applicant said that she had not distributed flyers and she did not know why the police suspected her.

propositions.text: She could not explain why she wrote about distributing flyers in her BOC.
propositions.quote: She could not explain why she had written that she had been arrested for distributing flyers in her BOC.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the applicant inconsistent about reasons for arrest and unable to explain the contradiction.

propositions.text: The applicant did not offer credible testimony about being followed by government officials; testimony was vague and general without specific examples.
propositions.quote: Third, the applicant did not offer credible testimony on being followed by government officials. In her BOC, she alleged that she had been followed for about two months. When asked to provide examples at the hearing, she offered very general and vague testimony. She could not describe a single specific example or incident.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the applicant’s testimony about being followed was vague, general, and lacked specific examples, thus not credible.

propositions.text: There were inconsistencies between the applicant’s detailed BOC knowledge of husband’s activities and vague oral testimony.
propositions.quote: Finally, the panel noted that there were inconsistencies between the applicant’s knowledge of her husband’s activities as expressed in her BOC and her oral testimony. In the BOC, she provided a detailed account of her husband’s activities, replete with dates and background information on the OLF. However, her oral testimony was vague and ambiguous.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found inconsistencies between the applicant’s detailed BOC and vague oral testimony about her husband’s activities.

propositions.text: The RPD concluded the applicant’s allegations lacked credibility and found no serious possibility of persecution.
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded that the applicant’s allegations lacked credibility. It determined that there was no serious possibility that the applicant would be persecuted.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, the RPD found no risk of torture, risk to life, or cruel and unusual punishment in Ethiopia.
propositions.quote: It further determined, on the balance of probabilities, that she would not face torture or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual punishment in Ethiopia.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the applicant not credible and no serious risk of persecution or torture in Ethiopia on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: The applicant provided new evidence on appeal: affidavit, audiologist’s report, letter from friend, and internet article about hearing loss.
propositions.quote: In her appeal to the RAD, the applicant provided the following pieces of new evidence: 1. An affidavit she swore; 2. An audiologist’s report; 3. A letter from a friend dated August 1, 2013; and 4. An article printed from the Internet about hearing loss.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant submitted new evidence on appeal including affidavit, audiologist report, letter, and internet article about hearing loss.

propositions.text: The RAD uses the Raza test for admissibility of new evidence: credibility, newness, relevance, and materiality.
propositions.quote: He explains that he will use the test developed in the context of Pre-Removal Risk Assessment applications [PRRAs] in Raza v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 [Raza]. Evidence is admissible if it meets four criteria: credibility, newness, relevance and materiality.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD applies the Raza test requiring credibility, newness, relevance, and materiality for new evidence admissibility.

propositions.text: The applicant’s affidavit states hearing impairment from second imprisonment and son’s call about authorities searching for him.
propositions.quote: It states (1) that her hearing became impaired when she was struck on her left ear during her second term of imprisonment and (2) that her son called her a few weeks after the RPD hearing to tell her that the authorities were searching for him.

propositions.text: The RAD rejects the affidavit as the hearing impairment was known at the RPD hearing and no accommodation was requested.
propositions.quote: The RAD does not accept the affidavit, since the applicant would have been aware of any hearing impairment at the time of the hearing and could have given that evidence to the RPD. There was no indication in the RPD record that the applicant raised the issue or required accommodation for her hearing loss.

propositions.text: The son’s call lacks probative value as it concerns the son, not the applicant, failing the Raza test.
propositions.quote: The second piece of information fails the Raza test because it lacks probative value. It indicates that the authorities are looking for the applicant’s son, not the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD rejects the affidavit as the hearing impairment was known and the son’s call lacks probative value about the applicant.

propositions.text: The RAD excludes the letter from friend and internet article as vague, lacking probative value, and general in nature.
propositions.quote: The letter from the friend was written after the RPD decision but it did not meet the relevance test as it was vague and lacked probative value. The Internet article contained no date and was of a general nature about improving communication when there was hearing loss.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD excludes the friend’s letter and internet article as vague, irrelevant, and lacking probative value.

propositions.text: The applicant tendered a letter from her son dated December 15, 2013, received January 14, 2014, inquiring about her health and stating husband is alive and probably joined OLF.
propositions.quote: It is dated December 15, 2013. The applicant received it on January 14, 2014. The author inquires into the applicant’s health; states that her husband is alive and probably joined the OLF; and affirms that he plans to travel to South Africa himself to claim refugee protection.

propositions.text: The son’s letter does not allege anyone is looking for the applicant.
propositions.quote: The writer does not allege that anyone is looking for the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant tendered a son’s letter stating husband alive and planning to claim refugee protection; no allegation anyone seeks the applicant.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the son’s letter does not provide new evidence to alter the RPD decision and is inadmissible under Rule 29.
propositions.quote: According to the RAD, the letter does not provide any new evidence which would justify altering the RPD decision. Nor has the applicant provided an explanation as to why she was unable to obtain or tender this document at an earlier point in time. The letter is inadmissible under Rule 29 and so a full Raza analysis is not necessary.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the son’s letter inadmissible under Rule 29 and not new evidence to alter the RPD decision.

propositions.text: The RAD conducted a standard of review analysis and concluded the standard of reasonableness governs the appeal.
propositions.quote: The RAD member then conducts a lengthy standard of review analysis. He concludes that the standard of reasonableness governs the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concluded the standard of reasonableness applies to the appeal after analysis.

propositions.text: The applicant alleges the RPD erred by failing to consider documentary evidence including letter from Ali Keder, affidavit from Konjit Mitiku, country conditions evidence, and UDJ receipt.
propositions.quote: The applicant alleged that the RPD erred in failing to consider documentary evidence in support of her claim, including a letter from Ali Keder, an affidavit from Konjit Mitiku and objective country conditions evidence. The RPD also took no consideration of a receipt from the UJD party corroborating a donation she had made to it.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges the RPD erred by not considering various documentary evidence supporting her claim.

propositions.text: The RPD is not required to refer to every piece of evidence; error occurs only if important evidence on a central issue is omitted
propositions.quote: The RAD recalls that the RPD is not required to refer to each and every piece of evidence before it. A reviewable error occurs only where the RPD omits to mention important evidence that is directly relevant to a central issue.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD recalls the RPD need not mention all evidence; error arises only if important evidence on a central issue is omitted.

propositions.text: No error occurred regarding the letter from Ali Keder as it referred to 2012 arrest, not central 2013 arrest issue
propositions.quote: The RAD is satisfied that no error occurred with respect to the letter from Ali Keder, as it refers to the arrest in 2012. By contrast, the RPD’s credibility findings related only to the arrest in 2013. The letter did not speak to an issue central to the decision.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found no error about the letter from Ali Keder since it concerned 2012 arrest, not the 2013 arrest central to credibility findings.

propositions.text: RPD failed to mention important evidence: affidavit of Konjit Mitiku, donation receipt, and country conditions evidence
propositions.quote: The RAD accepts that some important pieces of evidence were not mentioned in the RPD decision, specifically the affidavit where Konjit Mitiku swears to have visited the applicant while she was in prison, the receipt of the donation to the UDJ and the country conditions evidence.

propositions.text: It was unreasonable for the RPD to analyze the case without mentioning this important evidence
propositions.quote: The RAD determines that it was unreasonable for the RPD to conduct its analysis without mentioning this evidence in its reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the RPD unreasonably omitted important evidence including an affidavit, donation receipt, and country conditions evidence.

propositions.text: The RPD conducted a section 97 risk assessment despite applicant's claim otherwise
propositions.quote: The language used by the RPD shows that it did conduct a section 97 assessment in the RAD’s view.

propositions.text: Applicant's lack of credibility was fatal to claims under both sections 96 and 97
propositions.quote: The applicant’s lack of credibility was equally fatal to her claim under section 96 and section 97.

propositions.text: Negative credibility finding under section 96 may obviate need to consider section 97
propositions.quote: It is trite law that a negative credibility finding in relation to section 96 may obviate the need to consider section 97.

propositions.text: Given credibility concerns, the RPD's brief section 97 analysis was reasonable
propositions.quote: Given the RPD’s concerns with the applicant’s credibility, the cursory nature of its section 97 analysis was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the RPD did conduct a section 97 assessment; credibility issues made detailed section 97 analysis unnecessary and reasonable.

propositions.text: The RPD's credibility findings withstand reasonableness review and are confirmed by the RAD
propositions.quote: In light of the numerous concerns identified by the RPD and the deference which credibility findings deserve, the RAD concludes that these findings pass muster on the standard of reasonableness. Consequently, the RAD confirms the RPD’s decision.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirmed the RPD's credibility findings as reasonable and upheld the decision.

propositions.text: This application raises three issues: RAD's standard of review, analysis of new evidence, and analysis of credibility
propositions.quote: This application raises three issues: 1. Did the RAD err in its standard of review analysis? 2. Did the RAD err in its analysis of the new evidence? 3. Did the RAD err in its analysis of credibility?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies three issues: errors in RAD's standard of review, new evidence analysis, and credibility analysis.

propositions.text: There is differing jurisprudence on the standard of review the Court should apply to RAD's choice of standard of review
propositions.quote: The standard of review which the Court ought to apply to the RAD’s selection of a standard of review is the subject of differing jurisprudence in this Court.

propositions.text: Huruglica case applied correctness standard to RAD's choice of standard of review as a legal question of general interest
propositions.quote: In Huruglica v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 799 at paras 25-34, Justice Phelan selected the standard of correctness, characterizing the RAD’s choice of a standard of review as a question of law of general interest to the legal system.

propositions.text: Other cases preferred reasonableness standard, viewing it as a legal question within decision-maker's expertise
propositions.quote: Other members of the Court have taken a different view and preferred the standard of reasonableness, characterizing the issue as a legal question within the expertise of the decision-maker: see e.g. Akuffo v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1063 and Djossou v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1080.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes conflicting jurisprudence on the standard of review for RAD's choice: Huruglica applies correctness, others reasonableness.

propositions.text: No need to decide the standard of review issue here; Court of Appeal will address it soon
propositions.quote: I do not deem it necessary to express an opinion on this matter in this case. As an appeal has been brought against Huruglica, the Court of Appeal will soon have an opportunity to answer this question.

propositions.text: Nothing turns on the Court-to-RAD standard of review here as RAD's deferential choice was correct and reasonable
propositions.quote: In any event, nothing turns on the Court-to-RAD standard of review here, since the RAD’s selection of a deferential standard of review was both correct and reasonable, as I explain below.

paragraphs.summary: The court declines to decide the standard of review issue, finding RAD's deferential choice correct and reasonable.

propositions.text: Standard of review for RAD's application of statute and facts is reasonableness
propositions.quote: The standard of review for the second issue is reasonableness, as it involves the RAD’s application of its home statute and regulations to the facts before it: Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at paras 53-54.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review for RAD's application of statute to facts is reasonableness.

propositions.text: RAD's confirmation of RPD's credibility findings is reviewed on reasonableness standard
propositions.quote: The RAD did not make independent credibility findings. Rather, it confirmed the credibility findings made by the RPD. Since this required the RAD to evaluate the facts before it in light of its enabling statute, the Court-to-RAD standard of review is reasonableness again.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD's confirmation of RPD credibility findings is reviewed on reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: RAD committed no error deferring to RPD's fact and credibility findings despite debate on standard of review
propositions.quote: The RAD committed no error in deferring to the RPD’s findings on questions of fact and credibility despite the live debate in this Court on the appropriate standard of review,

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD did not err in deferring to RPD's fact and credibility findings despite debate on standard of review.

propositions.text: Court has sent back decisions where RAD deferred to RPD on state protection and plausibility/generalized risk issues
propositions.quote: The Court has sent back decisions where the RAD showed deference on different issues. For instance, in Huruglica, the RAD deferred to the RPD’s state protection analysis. In Alyafi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 952, the RAD deferred to the RPD’s findings on plausibility but also generalized risk – the latter was a question of mixed fact and law.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes prior cases where RAD deferred to RPD on state protection and plausibility/generalized risk issues.

propositions.text: Both jurisprudential strands accept deference to credibility findings as RAD lacks oral hearing advantage
propositions.quote: Yet both strands in the jurisprudence accept the principle that findings of credibility must be shown deference, since the RAD does not typically hold oral hearings and is therefore at a disadvantage in comparison to the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court states both jurisprudential views accept deference to credibility findings due to RAD's lack of oral hearings.

propositions.text: Huruglica views RAD as appeal de novo but recognizes need for deference on credibility
propositions.quote: In Huruglica, Justice Phelan expressed the view that the RAD scheme functions as an appeal de novo. Yet he recognized the need for deference when credibility is at issue (para 37).

propositions.text: Huruglica rejects palpable and overriding error standard for credibility, implicitly endorsing reasonableness
propositions.quote: Furthermore, he stated that the standard of review for credibility is not “palpable and overriding error” (paras 54-55). On my interpretation, he implicitly endorsed the standard of reasonableness, as that is the most common deferential standard in our law.

paragraphs.summary: Huruglica sees RAD as appeal de novo but endorses deference on credibility and reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Spasoja views RAD as appellate court applying palpable and overriding error standard on credibility
propositions.quote: In Spasoja v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 913 at para 39, Justice Roy took the view that the RAD functions like an appellate court, relying on the analytical framework in Barreau (Québec) c Québec (Tribunal des professions), 2011 QCCA 1498. When credibility findings are at issue, he asserted that the RAD ought to apply the standard of review of “palpable and overriding error”.

paragraphs.summary: Spasoja views RAD as appellate court applying palpable and overriding error standard on credibility.

propositions.text: The debate on standard of review is academic as neither side supports correctness standard
propositions.quote: This debate is largely academic because neither side would agree with the applicant that the standard of correctness applies.

propositions.text: If RAD erred by naming reasonableness instead of palpable and overriding error, it is immaterial
propositions.quote: If the RAD erred by naming the deferential standard it chose “reasonableness” instead of “palpable and overriding error”, nothing turns on it.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the debate on standard of review academic; naming reasonableness instead of palpable and overriding error is immaterial.

propositions.text: Justice Noël questioned RAD's deference to RPD on credibility, suggesting RAD should reassess credibility
propositions.quote: Shortly before the hearing, the applicant brought to my attention a recent case decided by my brother Justice Simon Noël: Khachatourian v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 182. In comments made in obiter at paras 30-34, Justice Noël questioned the wisdom of allowing the RAD to defer to the RPD’s findings, even on questions of credibility.

propositions.text: The court agrees with Justice Noël that RAD is not a judicial review body and deplores language suggesting so
propositions.quote: I agree with Justice Noël that an appellate tribunal does not play a judicial review function and deplore any language used by the RAD which points in that direction.

propositions.text: The court disagrees that RAD should routinely reassess credibility on appeal
propositions.quote: However, and with the greatest respect, I do not agree that the RAD should routinely conduct a fresh assessment of credibility on appeals brought before it.

paragraphs.summary: The court acknowledges Justice Noël's criticism of RAD's deference but disagrees that RAD should routinely reassess credibility.

propositions.text: It is difficult for RAD to apply correctness standard on credibility given RPD's advantage of observing claimant in person
propositions.quote: It is difficult to understand how an administrative tribunal could apply the standard of correctness to findings of credibility on a paper-based appeal. The RPD has a situational advantage when compared to the RAD, as it can observe the claimant in person while the RAD does not do so except in unusual circumstances.

propositions.text: If RAD owed no deference to RPD's credibility findings, the statutory scheme would be duplicative and RPD would lose purpose
propositions.quote: If the RAD owed no deference to the RPD’s findings on the issue which the RPD is best placed to decide, the statutory scheme would involve unnecessary duplication. The RPD would have no raison d’être.

propositions.text: This supports RAD-to-RPD deference on credibility issues
propositions.quote: This recommends RAD-to-RPD deference on issues of credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD should defer to RPD on credibility due to RPD's in-person advantage and to avoid duplication.

propositions.text: The RAD made its own credibility assessment relying on RPD's thorough discussion of inconsistencies
propositions.quote: I am satisfied, in any event, that the RAD made its own assessment of the applicant’s credibility relying on the very thorough discussion by the RPD of the inconsistencies which it had found between her BOC and testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD made its own credibility assessment based on RPD's thorough discussion of inconsistencies.

propositions.text: RAD may apply Raza factors from PRRAs when applying new evidence rule in subsection 110(4)
propositions.quote: The RAD was entitled to import the Raza factors established for PRRAs when applying the new evidence rule in subsection 110(4).

propositions.text: Iyamuremye held it reasonable for RAD to use Raza factors to analyze admissibility of fresh evidence under subsection 110(4)
propositions.quote: In Iyamuremye v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 494 at para 45, Justice Shore held that: Considering the dearth of case law interpreting subsection 110(4) and given the essential similarity between the provisions in question, the Court does not find it unreasonable for the RAD to have referred to the factors set out in Raza, above, to analyse the admissibility of fresh evidence.

propositions.text: Raza case law established legal meaning of 'new evidence' consistent with Parliament's intent in subsection 110(4)
propositions.quote: This case law established a legal meaning to the general application of the words “new evidence,” which, in the Court’s view, is consistent with Parliament’s clear intention with regard to subsection 110(4) to require that the RAD review the RPD’s decision as is, unless new, credible and relevant evidence arose after the rejection, that might have affected the outcome of the RPD hearing if that evidence had been presented to it.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD properly applied Raza factors for new evidence under subsection 110(4), consistent with Iyamuremye and Parliament's intent.

propositions.text: The RAD relied on Rule 29(4) to exclude new evidence after the appeal record was filed.
propositions.quote: the RAD relied on the express language of Rule 29(4) to exclude new evidence tendered after the appeal record was filed

propositions.text: Rule 29(4) explicitly lists some of the Raza factors.
propositions.quote: That Rule explicitly lists some of the Raza factors

paragraphs.summary: The RAD excluded new evidence after filing under Rule 29(4), which lists some Raza factors, as found by the RAD.

propositions.text: Justice Simon Noël expressed reservations about applying Raza to the RAD context in Khachatourian.
propositions.quote: Justice Simon Noël expressed reservations about the propriety of transposing Raza to the RAD context

propositions.text: I respectfully disagree with Justice Noël's reservations about applying Raza to the RAD context.
propositions.quote: Once again, I respectfully disagree

propositions.text: Justice Shore observed subsections 110(4) and 113(a) contain virtually identical language.
propositions.quote: As Justice Shore observed in Iyamuremye, subsections 110(4) and 113(a) contain virtually identical language

propositions.text: I give no significance to the slight discrepancy in the French text between the two provisions.
propositions.quote: I accord no significance to the slight discrepancy in the French text

paragraphs.summary: Justice Noël questioned applying Raza to RAD; I disagree, noting Shore's observation of identical language and no significance to French text differences.

propositions.text: Court must prioritize written text absent lexical ambiguity when interpreting legislative intent.
propositions.quote: When interpreting legislative intent, the Court must give priority to the written text in the absence of any lexical ambiguity

propositions.text: Court's policy opinions cannot override law text or select Hansard passages.
propositions.quote: The Court’s opinions on best policy cannot supplant the text of the law; nor can select passages from the Hansard

propositions.text: Parliament intended the two provisions to enshrine the same legal test.
propositions.quote: In my view, Parliament intended these two provisions to enshrine the same legal test

propositions.text: If Parliament intended more flexible RAD admissibility rules, it would not have replicated restrictive PRRA language.
propositions.quote: If Parliament had intended to establish more flexible admissibility rules in RAD appeals, it would not have replicated the restrictive language which governs PRRAs

paragraphs.summary: Court prioritizes text over policy or Hansard, finds Parliament intended same legal test in both provisions, not flexible RAD rules.

propositions.text: I am satisfied the RAD reasonably excluded the contested evidence for its reasons.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the RAD reasonably excluded the contested evidence for the reasons it provided

propositions.text: Applicant focused on RAD’s exclusion of her son’s letter under Rule 29(4).
propositions.quote: The applicant focused on the RAD’s exclusion of her son’s letter under Rule 29(4)

propositions.text: RAD reasonably excluded the letter due to low relevance and probative value and concerns it could have been available earlier.
propositions.quote: the RAD reasonably excluded the letter due to its low relevance and probative value. It also expressed reasonable concerns that the letter could have been available earlier

paragraphs.summary: I find RAD reasonably excluded evidence, including son’s letter, due to low relevance and availability concerns, despite applicant’s focus on exclusion.

propositions.text: RPD based negative credibility findings on inconsistencies between BOC narrative and oral testimony.
propositions.quote: The RPD based its numerous negative credibility findings on significant inconsistencies and contradictions between the applicant’s BOC narrative and her oral testimony

propositions.text: Applicant did not dispute RPD’s credibility findings at RAD or judicial review but argued RPD erred by ignoring corroborating documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The applicant did not dispute these findings during her appeal at the RAD, nor has she done so on this judicial review application. Rather, she insists that the RPD erred by failing to consider documentary evidence which corroborates her allegations

paragraphs.summary: RPD found applicant not credible due to inconsistencies; applicant did not dispute this but argued RPD ignored corroborating evidence.

propositions.text: RAD agreed RPD unreasonably failed to mention some evidence but upheld credibility findings as reasonable.
propositions.quote: the RAD ultimately upheld the RPD’s conclusions because its credibility findings were reasonable in light of the record

propositions.text: RAD committed no reviewable error in upholding RPD’s credibility findings despite omission of some evidence.
propositions.quote: The RAD committed no reviewable error in this regard

paragraphs.summary: RAD found RPD unreasonably omitted some evidence but upheld credibility findings; I find no reviewable error by RAD.

propositions.text: In Kanto, RPD erred on state protection but credibility finding was reasonable and judicial review dismissed.
propositions.quote: Justice de Montigny found that the RPD had erred in its state protection analysis but had still reasonably concluded that the applicants lacked credibility

propositions.text: Negative credibility finding can render state protection error immaterial and justify dismissal of judicial review.
propositions.quote: Although the Applicants have demonstrated an error in the assessment of state protection, it is of no consequence because they have failed to establish that they are in need of that protection

paragraphs.summary: Kanto case held RPD’s state protection error immaterial due to reasonable negative credibility finding, leading to dismissal.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably found RPD’s error immaterial due to applicant’s lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD implicitly and reasonably determined that the RPD’s error was immaterial due to the applicant’s lack of credibility

propositions.text: Unmentioned evidence could not remedy contradictions in applicant’s testimony.
propositions.quote: It was reasonable for the RAD to conclude that the unmentioned evidence could not remedy the significant contradictions and inconsistencies in the applicant’s testimony

propositions.text: Applicant’s counsel argued RAD should have given weight to affidavit of Konjit Mikitu.
propositions.quote: counsel for the applicant forcefully argued at the hearing that the RAD should have given some weight to the affidavit of Konjit Mikitu

propositions.text: Failure to give weight to affidavit does not establish reviewable error on reasonableness review.
propositions.quote: the failure do so does not establish a reviewable error in my view

paragraphs.summary: I find RAD reasonably deemed RPD’s error immaterial due to lack of credibility; failure to weigh affidavit is not reviewable error.

propositions.text: Applicant’s counsel reproached RAD for endorsing RPD’s credibility findings without detailed explanation.
propositions.quote: Counsel for the applicant also reproached the RAD for summarily endorsing the RPD’s credibility findings

propositions.text: Counsel seeks to impose unnecessary requirement on RAD to restate RPD’s well-explained inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: he seeks to impose a pro forma and unnecessary requirement on the RAD to restate in different words what the RPD had so convincingly explained

propositions.text: RPD’s statement of inconsistencies spoke for itself.
propositions.quote: The RPD’s statement of the inconsistencies spoke for itself

paragraphs.summary: Applicant’s counsel criticized RAD’s brief endorsement of RPD’s credibility findings; I find no need for RAD to restate RPD’s clear inconsistencies.

propositions.text: RAD’s endorsement of RPD’s section 97 analysis was reasonable.
propositions.quote: Similarly, the RAD’s endorsement of the RPD’s section 97 analysis was reasonable

propositions.text: Negative credibility finding may obviate need to consider section 97 (Ache).
propositions.quote: a negative credibility finding may obviate the need to consider section 97

propositions.text: Board’s general finding of lack of credibility suffices to dispose claim unless independent credible evidence supports claim (Sellan).
propositions.quote: where the Board makes a general finding that the claimant lacks credibility, that determination is sufficient to dispose of the claim unless there is independent and credible documentary evidence

propositions.text: Claimant bears onus to show independent credible evidence exists to support claim (Sellan).
propositions.quote: The claimant bears the onus of demonstrating there was such evidence

paragraphs.summary: RAD reasonably endorsed RPD’s section 97 analysis; negative credibility can end claim unless claimant shows independent credible evidence, who bears onus.

propositions.text: Applicant provided no independent credible evidence showing risk in Ethiopia.
propositions.quote: the applicant provided no independent and credible evidence to show that she faces risk in Ethiopia

propositions.text: Objective evidence describes risks faced by political dissidents and families.
propositions.quote: The objective documentary evidence describes risks faced by political dissidents and their families

propositions.text: RPD did not believe applicant or husband were political dissidents.
propositions.quote: The RPD questioned the applicant’s credibility and did not believe that either she or her husband were political dissidents

propositions.text: Applicant lacks profile placing her at risk; RAD committed no error confirming RPD’s analysis.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the applicant does not have a profile that places her at risk. The RAD committed no error in confirming the RPD’s analysis in this respect

paragraphs.summary: Applicant gave no credible evidence of risk; RPD disbelieved political dissident status; RAD rightly confirmed RPD’s analysis.

propositions.text: Application is dismissed; no questions for certification proposed or certified.
propositions.quote: This application is dismissed. The parties did not propose questions for certification and none will be certified

paragraphs.summary: Application dismissed; no certification questions proposed or certified by court.
